item.title: The War of 1812 and the Monroe Doctrine, 1807–1823
item.snippet: War of 1812 battles, Latin American independence and US recognition, and the 1819 boundary with the land Spain gave up.
item.description:
Question: Why did the United States go to war in 1812, and what did the Monroe Doctrine claim?

Ideas for one lesson in MapMaker (choose any):

  • Choose three War of 1812 battles and explain why each was fought where it was. Sketch the British blockade along the coast, and a pin at Ghent, where the peace treaty was signed in December 1814.
  • Switch on Latin American independence: when did each nation become independent, and when did the United States recognize it? Compare the dates with the Monroe Doctrine (1823), and sketch the area it covered.
  • Switch on Adams–Onís Treaty line, 1819 and Land Spain gave up in 1819 to see what the treaty settled.
  • Download an image or export a PDF of the map to keep the work.

Notes: The 1819 line is drawn from the treaty's description on Natural Earth's rivers, so it's approximate. In the treaty Spain ceded East Florida and gave up its claim to West Florida, which the United States had claimed as part of the Louisiana Purchase after American settlers there rebelled in 1810; the treaty was ratified in 1821 (Office of the Historian). The national boundaries layer, from the War of 1812 Battles map, shows 1800, before the Louisiana Purchase. Recognition dates come from the Office of the Historian, and so do independence dates, except Mexico's and Brazil's, which come from the Library of Congress country studies. Chile celebrates 18 September 1810 as independence day (both sources) and won formal independence in 1818 (Library of Congress).

Sources: American Battlefield Trust (battles) and National Park Service (battlefield boundaries), from the War of 1812 Battles map; University of Minnesota (national boundaries, 1800); MapMaker catalogue (territorial acquisitions); Office of the Historian, U.S. Department of State; Library of Congress (country studies); Avalon Project, Yale Law School (treaty text); Natural Earth.

Version 1.2 (14 October 2026).

item.title: Historical National Boundaries
item.snippet: Historical national boundaries for key years in history, including 1800, 1914, 1918, 1939, 1945, 1970, 1990, and 2000.
item.description:
Historical National Boundaries displays global national boundaries for the following dates in history: 1800, 1914, 1918, 1939, 1945, 1970, 1990, 2000. Boundary changes associated with World War I (1914 - 1918) and World War II (1939 - 1945) can be viewed by turning off all other layers and toggling between the two.

Data for each layer comes from a variety of sources, including historical atlases and the Library of Congress website - https://www.loc.gov/maps/.

item.title: United States Territorial Acquisitions
item.snippet: This layer by the U.S. Geological Survey and the U.S. Department of the Interior shows territorial acquisitions made by the United States from the post-Revolutionary War era through its current boundaries, which were established in 1917.
item.description:
The nation we now know as the United States was built slowly, over time. This layer shows how the territory that now forms the U.S. was shaped by a series of purchases, treaties, battles, and migration. 

It is important to acknowledge that this map only shows land acquisitions from a Western colonial perspective. It focuses on the acquisition of land from other Western nations’ colonial claims. It does not show land taken from Indigenous Nations, whether by treaty, theft, forced relocation, or other means. Please use this layer together with the Indigenous Territories layer to map a more complete picture of the Indigenous Nations who lived on these lands prior to European and other Western settlement. 

This layer is based on a map provided by the U.S. Department of the Interior and the U.S. Geological Survey. Some areas were disputed and have more than one treaty listed. In these cases, the later date was used to show when the area became part of the U.S. For example, at the time when the United States and France negotiated the Louisiana Purchase, no Western nations had actually explored or mapped the territory, and so the boundary between the Spanish and French territorial holdings had never been defined. French and American negotiators never settled on an official western boundary, leaving ownership of this portion of the Louisiana territory to be contested by Spain and later Mexico. These areas were officially acquired by the U.S. through the Annexation of Texas, formalized by the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo, following the Mexican-American War. 

Data Citation: U.S. Department of the Interior and the U.S. Geological Survey, Territorial Acquisitions Map, 2014, https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/sis/resources/maps/territorial-acquisitions.html.

item.title: United States Battlefield Boundaries
item.snippet: This map layer shows the footprint of historic U.S. battlefields from the Revolutionary War (1775-1783), the War of 1812, and the Civil War (1861-1865) that are part of the National Park Service’s American Battlefield Protection Program.
item.description:
A battlefield is the current or historic location where an armed conflict or military battle takes place. You might be picturing an open field with soldiers based on the name. However, a battlefield is any place where a battle has taken place. For example, the Wilderness battle (May 5th to 7th, 1864) in the state of Virginia during the Civil War was fought in dense woodland. 

 

Many people consider battlefields to be sacred sites or hallowed ground. This is because of the number of people who died there in the conflict. Many people travel to these places to learn and honor the soldiers who sacrificed there.

 

This map layer shows the historic battlefields in the United States included in the National Park Service’s American Battlefield Protection Program. This program works to preserve and provide interpretation of these important places. By studying the past, we can learn from it and hopefully learn from the past mistakes of others. 

 

This map layer includes battlefields from 3 wars: the Revolutionary War (1775-1783), the War of 1812, and the Civil War (1861-1865). This layer includes two parts: one, the footprint of the entire battlefield, and two, the core area, where the fighting was the heaviest. The data for this map comes from two separate reports: the Report to Congress on the Historic Preservation of Revolutionary War and War of 1812 Sites in the United States (2007) and the Civil War Sites Advisory Commission Report on the Nation’s Civil War Battlefields (1993). 

 

Note: You are likely viewing this layer as part of a map on a specific war or battle. In that case, you may only see the battlefields for the specific event and not all three wars included in this dataset. This is not an error; the map maker has simply filtered the data to keep the map clear and concise.

item.title: Adams–Onís Treaty line, 1819
item.snippet: The 1819 boundary between the United States and Spanish lands, from the Gulf of Mexico to the Pacific.
item.description:
Seven parts following Article 3 of the treaty: up the Sabine to 32° N, north to the Red River, up the Red to 100° W, north to the Arkansas, up the Arkansas to its source, north to 42° N and west along 42° N to the Pacific.

Drawn from the treaty's description on Natural Earth's rivers: approximate at classroom scale.

Version 1.0 (14 October 2026).

item.title: Battles of the War of 1812
item.snippet: Explore the major battles of the War of 1812 (1812 to 1815) with this map layer by the American Battlefield Trust, which works to preserve endangered battlefields across the United States.
item.description:
This layer, compiled by the American Battlefield Trust, shows the battles fought during the War of 1812. The War of 1812 is sometimes called the Second War of Independence. Britain and France were at war, and both were attempting to restrict the United States from trading with the other. France was a major trading partner for the United States. Britain was also stopping U.S. ships at sea, forcing their sailors to join the Royal Navy. Enraged, the U.S., under President James Madison, prepared for war. 

The U.S. Navy won several battles against the British Royal Navy, especially in the Great Lakes region. But the army was less successful. The U.S. Army attempted several times to invade Canada, primarily around Buffalo, New York, and Niagara Falls. At the time, the U.S. Army was small and poorly trained compared to Britain’s forces. It was supplemented by state militias, which often lacked sufficient weapons or supplies.

In 1814, when the war with France temporarily ended, additional British forces landed in Maryland. This army marched through Washington, D.C., burning public buildings, before trying to capture Baltimore. From there, they moved south. By the end of the war, British troops were quartered in the Spanish territory in Florida. Jackson pursued them there, but by the time he fought them in the Battle of New Orleans, the Treaty of Ghent had officially ended the war.

Data Citation: American Battlefield Trust. Maps. 2025 https://www.battlefields.org/search?algolia_search_index%5BrefinementList%5D%5Bfield_resource_type%5D%5B0%5D=map&ms=googlepaid&ms=googlepaid.
